The Attractiveness of Growth

 What is growth and why measure it?
 Student learning is a central goal of education.
 Assessments of student achievement provide evidence of
 the current status of student knowledge and
 understanding.
 Learning is demonstrated by growth in student
 achievement from one point in time to another point in
 time–not by status at either point time alone.

Guiding Questions
 Growth models address specific questions
 Different growth analysis techniques are good at
 answering different questions.
 It is critical to understand these different questions.
 Different questions lead to different conversations which
 lead to different uses and outcomes.

 Changing conversations about education
 Starting with the right questions simplifies development
 and motivating the proper use of the growth model results.
 The questions set the table for those conversations. See
 Yen (2007) for an excellent list of questions derived from a
 survey of parents, teachers and administrators

The Rhode Island Growth Model

 How much growth did a student make? Is it enough?
 The Rhode Island Growth Model uses Student Growth
 Percentiles [Betebenner, 2008, Betebenner, 2009] to
 quantify individual student growth.
 This approach was developed and used by Colorado and
 is currently being employed in Massachusetts, Indiana,
 Virginia, and more than a dozen other states.
 Rhode Island has been investigating the model for uses
 with school improvement for the last 2 years.
 An important aspect of the model is that it separates the
 description of growth from discussions of
 responsibility/accountability.

Describing Student Growth

 Discussing student growth, even with a vertical scale (which
 NECAP does not possess), is not a simple task.
 Some believe a vertical scale simplifies the task of measuring
 student growth.
 Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth and change
 require context. Consider, for example, height.
 A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
 4 inches is a well understood quantity.
 The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when
 understood alongside the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
 Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a
 norm-referenced basis for describing student growth.

Student Growth Percentiles

 Should we be surprised with a child’s current achievement given
 their prior achievement?
 Student growth percentiles (SGPs) answer this question.
 Consider a low achieving student with 90th percentile growth
 and a high achieving student with 10th percentile growth.
 The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 90 percent
 of similar students.
 The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 10
 percent of similar students.
 The low achiever’s growth is more exemplary (probabilistically)
 than the high achiever’s.
 Judgments about the adequacy of student growth require
 external criteria together with standard setting.

From Students to Groups of Students
 Aristotle
 We understand best those things we see emerge from their very
 beginnings.

 It’s of interest to examine teachers and schools where
 students demonstrate, on average, extraordinarily high and
 low student growth.
 To summarize the student growth percentiles (SGPs)
 associated with a school (or other grouping) one calculates
 the median of the student growth percentiles.
 Median SGPs can be calculated for one or several years
 across single and multiple subjects.

Growth, Effectiveness, and Value-Added

 Fundamental Premise
 “Good” schools or teachers bring about student growth in ex-
 cess of that found at “bad” schools or teachers.

 In Rhode Island, “good” teachers are called highly effective
 teachers.
 What’s the relationship between growth and effectiveness?
 Effectiveness indicates who/what is responsible for the growth
 (value-added models).
 Assuming the above premise is, at least, partly true. How do
 we judge the correctness of a value-added model?

Next Steps for Growth Data in Rhode Island

 Use of student growth for teacher evaluation has expedited
 work on and use of the Rhode Island Growth Model.
 RIDE is in the process of linking student NECAP data to
 unique teacher identifiers.
 In the coming weeks, RIDE will use preliminary teacher
 identifiers in a few districts to look at student growth for
 teachers.
 These preliminary results will be used to understand a range
 of issues including:
 The integrity of the teacher student links in the data files.
 The number of student NECAP results associated with
 teachers in a given year (minimum n).
 Empirical results to help set cuts distinguishing teacher
 performance.
